facts.title: Named for the Far North
facts.text: Thulium takes its name from Thule, the ancient Greek and Roman name for a mythical land at the northern edge of the known world, often associated with Scandinavia. The Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve coined the name in 1879 to honor his homeland. It is one of several elements (alongside scandium, holmium, and others) whose names trace back to Nordic geography.

facts.title: The Rarest Stable Lanthanide
facts.text: Among the lanthanides that are not radioactive, thulium is the least abundant in Earth's crust, present at roughly 0.5 parts per million. Despite this rarity, it is still more common than gold or platinum. Its scarcity historically made it one of the most expensive rare-earth elements to isolate in pure form.

facts.title: Untangled from a Mixture
facts.text: Cleve discovered thulium by carefully analyzing impurities in erbium oxide, the same chemical detective work that also revealed holmium. He noticed a brown residue with absorption lines that belonged to no known element. Isolating a reasonably pure sample, however, took decades: Charles James of the United States finally produced relatively clean thulium around 1911 after performing about 15,000 painstaking recrystallizations.

facts.title: A Portable X-ray Source
facts.text: When the isotope thulium-170 is created by bombarding natural thulium with neutrons in a reactor, it becomes radioactive and emits X-rays as it decays. This makes it useful in small, lightweight portable X-ray devices for inspecting machinery, welds, and even dental or medical imaging in remote settings. With a half-life of about 128 days, a single source remains useful for many months before needing replacement.

facts.title: It Glows Blue in Lasers
facts.text: Thulium-doped crystals and optical fibers produce laser light around 2 micrometers in wavelength, in the infrared range. These thulium lasers are prized in surgery, especially for delicate procedures on soft tissue and the prostate, because their wavelength is strongly absorbed by water and cuts cleanly with minimal bleeding. The same fiber lasers also serve in materials processing and atmospheric sensing.

facts.title: The Money in Euro Banknotes
facts.text: Thulium compounds fluoresce a soft blue under ultraviolet light, a property exploited as a security feature in some euro banknotes to thwart counterfeiters. Under a UV lamp, hidden markings light up that are invisible in ordinary daylight. This anti-forgery role is one of the few everyday applications most people unknowingly encounter.

facts.title: A Single Natural Isotope
facts.text: Natural thulium consists entirely of one stable isotope, thulium-169, making it a monoisotopic element. This is relatively unusual, as most elements occur as mixtures of several isotopes. Thulium-169 is also notable in nuclear medicine research as a target for producing the isotope thulium-170.

facts.title: Forged in Dying Stars
facts.text: Like other heavy elements, thulium was not made in the Big Bang but forged inside stars, primarily through the slow neutron-capture process (the s-process) in aging red giant stars. The element is then scattered into space when such stars shed their outer layers or explode. Every atom of thulium on Earth is therefore stellar debris incorporated into our planet as it formed.

facts.title: Strong and Lightly Magnetic
facts.text: Thulium is a silvery-gray metal soft enough to be cut with a knife, yet at very low temperatures it becomes one of the more strongly magnetic rare-earth metals, ordering its magnetic moments below about 32 kelvin. Researchers study thulium and its alloys for high-field magnets and specialized magnetic materials. Its combination of softness at room temperature and dramatic low-temperature behavior makes it a useful subject for solid-state physics.

facts.title: No Job in Living Things
facts.text: Thulium has no known biological role in any organism, and humans encounter only trace amounts through diet and the environment. Its soluble salts show low to moderate toxicity, while insoluble forms are considered essentially non-toxic. Because it is so rare and chemically locked away in minerals, thulium poses negligible risk in everyday life, though like all rare earths it should be handled with care in concentrated industrial settings.
